summary: This informational document presents a framework for fast reroute in IP or MPLS networks using encapsulation and forwarding to not-via addresses. It uses a single level of encapsulation and can protect unicast, multicast, and LDP traffic against link, router, and shared risk group failures, regardless of topology and metrics.

plainLanguage.summary: When a road closes, packets get a note saying "get there without using that road." This lets traffic switch instantly.

questions: ip fast reroute using not-via addresses
how does ip fast reroute work
what is an srlg in routing
subtitle: How a router can repair around a failure by tunnelling packets to an address that is reachable only 'not via' the broken part.

tldr.problem: When a link or router fails, only its neighbours know at first. They must still steer packets around the failure while the rest of the network is unaware of it.
tldr.mechanism: Each router advertises special 'not-via' addresses, each meaning 'this node, reached without crossing that failed component'. The router next to the failure encapsulates packets to the right not-via address and the tunnel end removes the wrapper.
tldr.outcome: In principle it repairs any single failure that does not partition the network, whatever the topology or metrics. The RFC says it is only an illustrative framework, not a protocol specification, and that there was no demand to deploy it.

today: RFC 6981 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted or updated. It states that it is not a protocol specification and that further work is needed before implementation or deployment. It builds on the IP Fast Reroute framework in RFC 5714.

sections.title: A Framework, Not a Protocol
sections.content:
RFC 6981 describes IP Fast Reroute (IPFRR) using not-via addresses. When a link or router fails, only its neighbours initially know. Those neighbours, the repairing routers, must steer packets to their destinations even though most routers are unaware of the failure.

Many fast reroute schemes cannot say which component failed, so how well they work depends on the topology. This one encapsulates the packet to an address that explicitly names the component to avoid. As long as the failure does not partition the network, a repair is always achieved.

The document is explicit that its mechanisms are purely illustrative and do not constitute a protocol specification. It is a snapshot of the Routing Area Working Group's work, published as a document of record. It also says that at the time there was no demand to deploy the technology, and that more work is needed before implementation or deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a written-down idea, not a finished rulebook. The idea is to tell the packet exactly which broken piece to stay away from.

sections.title: Not-Via Addresses and Repairs
sections.content:
In the RFC's example, router S normally sends traffic for destination D through P and then B. If S suspects P has failed, it encapsulates the packet to Bp, an address on B that is reachable only not via P. The path from S to Bp is installed as the shortest path from S to B that avoids P. At B the wrapper is removed and the packet continues to D.

For full protection, every neighbour of P needs a not-via address, and P needs one for each neighbour. These addresses are advertised in the routing protocol in a way that marks them as not-via addresses and not ordinary ones.

Only one level of encapsulation is needed. The RFC says this repairs any failure regardless of link metrics and asymmetry, except where the failure was a single point of failure that partitions the network, where no repair is possible. Because the decapsulating router is always closer to the destination than the encapsulating one, the packet does not loop.

A router may use an Equal-Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) repair in place of a not-via repair. The RFC also notes that Loop-Free Alternates (RFC 5286) need no extra addresses, upgrades or encapsulation, but only some destinations have one. It assumes LFAs are used where available and the rest are repaired with not-via, with the split being a local implementation choice.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a street address that only works if you drive around one particular closed bridge. The detour is already written into the address, so nobody needs to know the bridge is broken.

sections.title: Computing and Using Repairs
sections.content:
Every router on the repair path needs a route to the not-via address, and it cannot tell in advance whether it is on one. So each router pretends, one at a time, that each other router has failed, and computes its own route to the not-via addresses of that router's neighbours. Done naively this takes n-1 shortest path first (SPF) runs for n routers. The RFC uses incremental SPF, stopped once the nodes advertising the relevant not-via addresses are reattached. It reports that experiments on real-world topologies of 40 to 400 nodes suggest a worst case equal to between 5 and 13 full SPFs.

For a node failure, S encapsulates to the repair target, found by recording the next-next hop for each destination. For a link failure, S encapsulates to Ps (P not via S), and SHOULD send it on the shortest available path to P. Normal operation assumes router failure, and the link repair is for destinations reachable only through the failed router.

Packets already addressed to a not-via address are never repaired, so an unexpected second failure drops them rather than looping them. For multi-homed prefixes (reachable through more than one router), S chooses the closest router that can still reach the prefix and tunnels to it. That router MUST deliver the packet locally, so it cannot loop back through P.
sections.plainLanguage: Every router quietly rehearses 'what if that one broke?' for each neighbour ahead of time. When something really breaks, the answer is already on the shelf.

sections.title: Compound Failures
sections.content:
A Shared Risk Link Group (SRLG) is a set of links that one event, such as a conduit cut, can take down together. When repairing one member, all other members MUST be assumed failed, so the not-via address Ps now means 'P not via the link or any link sharing an SRLG with it'. Repairs for SRLG members in series use one level of encapsulation at a time, because each packet is decapsulated before it is re-encapsulated.

A LAN is treated as a special SRLG. The simplest option treats the LAN and all attached routers as failed. A finer option adds an address not via the LAN pseudonode and one extra address per router. A third option uses connectivity checks such as BFD (RFC 5880) to work out what really failed.

For multiple independent failures, repairs can loop if each repair path crosses the other failure. The basic scheme avoids loops by dropping repaired packets. Options include abandoning repair and using normal reconvergence (with the oFIB 'Abandoning All Hope' mechanism from RFC 6976), or advertising secondary SRLGs so that routers compute a repair avoiding both failures. The RFC also covers mixing LFAs and downstream routes with not-via, which needs extra care.
sections.plainLanguage: If two roads can close at once, the detour has to avoid both. If the detours would send cars in circles, it is safer to stop and let the usual map update take over.

sections.title: Multicast, MPLS, Encapsulation and Deployment
sections.content:
Multicast can be repaired much like unicast. The not-via address of the packet tells the forwarder the expected receive interface, so the Reverse Path Forwarding check still works. The RFC leaves a fuller description for further study.

For MPLS LDP networks, not-via addresses are IP addresses, so LDP (RFC 5036) distributes labels for them as usual. S pushes the repair endpoint's label for the destination, then the label for the not-via address. For a node repair, S needs the labels of its neighbours' neighbours.

Any IETF IP-in-IP encapsulation can carry a repair, including IP in IP (RFC 2003), GRE (RFC 1701) and L2TPv3 (RFC 3931), provided both ends support it. Care is needed so the tunnel does not push the packet past the MTU of the links it crosses.

Routing protocols would need extensions to advertise the not-via addresses, the ability to calculate not-via routes, and the encapsulation types supported. Incremental deployment is possible by leaving non-capable routers out of the base topology, so repairs steer around them. Routers that merely lie on a repair path need no forwarding changes.
sections.plainLanguage: The same trick works for group broadcasts and for label-based networks, and the wrapper can be one of several existing kinds. Old routers can be steered around while the new ones take over gradually.

sections.title: Security and Manageability
sections.content:
Repair endpoints could be abused to disguise delivery of a packet to a point in the network (RFC 6169). The primary protection SHOULD be a private address space for not-via addresses (RFC 1918, RFC 4193). Repair endpoint addresses MUST NOT be advertised outside the routing domain and MUST be filtered at network entry points.

An attacker might try to overload a router by sending heavy traffic to a decapsulation endpoint. The RFC notes that routers typically take a 50% performance penalty in decapsulating a packet and that the volume needed would be easy to detect. If an attacker can influence a link, they could trigger the repair, but a not-via network is less exposed to that than one doing full convergence on every link change.

The manageability section lists pre-failure configuration (for example, enabling protection per link or node), monitoring (such as notification of unprotectable links) and failure action monitoring (counts and logging of repairs). Ordinary tools such as ping and traceroute see not-via addresses as normal addresses, so they can verify repair paths.
sections.plainLanguage: The special addresses must stay inside your own network, like a private staff door. Keeping them hidden from outsiders stops anyone using them to sneak packets in.
